description: Turn the issue into product deliverables: who is served, what they can do, and how we would know it worked (feature.md §1). The uniform seven children of §0.2; every rule is about the child that just finished, so the state declares no transitions of its own.

## What a later phase sent back

{{.inputs.findings}}

A phase downstream of this one found the work does not hold up where they stand, which
is why control came back here.

That is a different reader from your own critique: they are looking at what your output
made *possible*, not at whether it is well made. A spec can be internally excellent and
still leave a flow unbuildable, a component ambiguous, or a test unwritable — and only
they can see it.

Shapes differ by sender. A review finding carries `severity` / `claim` / `lens`; a design
finding raised by acceptance or implementation carries whatever that phase recorded. Read
each entry for what it says rather than expecting one shape.

Fix what they name, or say plainly why they are wrong. Where a finding asks for something
this phase cannot produce, raise it as a `questions` entry rather than parking it.

Re-emit the deliverables in full, and record each finding in `responses`.

Turn the issue into product deliverables: who is served, what they can do, and
how we would know it worked.

## What a spec is

A spec **describes the product and answers the questions**. That is the whole of it.

It is not a record of how it came to be written. It never mentions a pass, a
revision, a draft, a critique, a finding, an earlier version of itself, or what
"this file previously" said. Write every document as though it were the first and
only one ever written, and as though the reader will never know a loop existed —
because they will not. If you change your mind later, the document simply *says the
new thing*; the account of what changed goes in `responses`, which is a run artifact
and is never published.

The sentences this rule forbids, so there is no doubt:

- "The previous version of this line got the attribution wrong."
- "This revision withdraws the amendment."
- "Two passes tried to generalise the last row."
- "An earlier draft carried an eighth row — it is removed rather than answered."
- "…on a narrower argument than the last pass gave."

Each of those is the loop talking about itself inside the deliverable. Delete the
scaffolding and keep the conclusion: not "the previous version said X, which was
wrong, because Y — so it is now Z", just **Z**, with the reason it is right.

**One deliverable, one file.** A document argues exactly one spec. If you find
yourself scoping a "floor" and a "delta" inside one doc, or naming a half that
could be cut on its own and priced on its own, that half is its **own** deliverable
— its own `features` row, its own importance, its own file. Two specs in one file
is the failure this rule exists to prevent.

**And one spec, one file.** Do not restate a spec's argument anywhere else. The
catalog gets a row and a link, never a second copy of the reasoning; a sibling doc
gets a cross-reference, never a rehearsal of the neighbour's case. If an argument
belongs to a feature, it lives in that feature's doc and nowhere else.

## Answer these, in order

1. **Who are we serving?** The user, a developer, support, marketing? Name one
   per deliverable, and name them the way they would describe themselves.
2. **What are the goals?** How does this bring value to that person? Can we
   measure that value — what does success look like, and what does failure look
   like?
3. **How does this feature bring that value?** What is necessary, what is
   sufficient, and what is merely nice to have?
4. **What other features must exist** for this one to deliver its value?
5. **Where does this sit among the features that already exist** — what does it
   overlap with, what does it make redundant, and what would a user expect it to
   do because of a neighbour?
6. **Does it conform to the product principles?** If not, this is an *exception*
   (with the reason, on the doc claiming it) or an *amendment* (the principle is
   wrong). Silence is neither, and phase 8 finds silent departures.

## What to produce

`features` — one entry per deliverable:

```
{ "id": "feature-name",
  "story": "As a [who], I should be able to [what] so that I can [value]",
  "importance": 0.0-1.0,
  "metrics": ["..."],
  "requires": ["other-feature-name"] }
```

Two things to get right in the story. The **who** has to be someone who would
recognise this as their job. The **so that I can** has to name something the
person wanted *before this feature existed* — "so that I can use the new panel"
is the feature wearing a story's clothes.

The metrics must measure the **value**, not the activity. Opens, clicks and
runs-started measure that the feature was reached. Ask which metric would move
if the feature were popular and useless, and do not write that one.

`feature_docs` — one doc per deliverable, on the `docs/_templates/product-feature.md`
template. Each carries its upward link, a **Where this fits** section (serves /
neighbors / depends on / history), and — where the exploration rejected a
reading — a **Framings considered** row.

`questions` — the product decisions you cannot take from the repo, and nobody has
taken for you. **This is the output that matters most on a first pass.** A question here
is answered in a sentence and closes an argument that would otherwise cost twenty minutes
of prose per pass.

```
{ "name": "chat-run-order__canceled-sort",
  "header": "Sort",
  "question": "Should a conversation you stopped yourself sort above the line with the unsettled ones, or below it with the finished ones?",
  "description": "The brief says \"uncompleted first\", which puts it above. The argument for below is that you already know about a thread you ended. It is one predicate member either way.",
  "options": [
    { "value": "above, as the brief says", "description": "the brief is honoured to the letter" },
    { "value": "below, with the finished", "description": "you ended it, so you can find it by name" }
  ],
  "default": "below, with the finished",
  "custom": true,
  "optional": true }
```

They are asked one at a time, each with your `default` already picked, a box for an
answer in the person's own words, and a way to pass.

Rules, all of them load-bearing:

- **Raise it only if a person can settle it and the repo cannot.** A question whose
  answer is in the code is not a question, it is a `read_file` you did not do.
- **Every entry is `optional: true` and `custom: true`.** A person who has no view must
  be able to pass, and a person whose answer is neither reading must be able to say so.
  Never add a "no view" option — passing is how that is said, and it comes back as an
  absent key rather than as a word you then have to know to ignore.
- **Give a `default`** — the reading you took, as one of the options' values. Answering
  is then confirming or overruling, never composing from nothing.
- **Spell the real alternatives out as `options`**, each with a `description` of what
  choosing it changes. Most product questions are a choice between two readings, not an
  essay.
- **`description` says what each answer would change.** A question a person cannot
  answer without reading the whole spec is a question you have not finished writing.
- **Ask about what you added, not only what you cut.** A thing you put in the
  *necessary* set that the brief never asked for is the question most worth asking,
  because approval would otherwise pass over it silently.
- **Keep it short.** Five questions a person will answer beat fifteen they will skip.
  Rank them and drop the tail.

Anything you raise here does **not** also go in the doc's **Open questions** table on
this pass — it is in flight. It returns to that table only if it comes back unanswered.

`doc_paths` — one path per entry in `features`, in the same order: `product/chat-run-order`
for `docs/product/chat-run-order.md`. Same length as `features`, always. If those two
lists differ in length you have either merged two specs into one file or split one across
two, and both are wrong.

`standing_amendment` — only when `product/principles.md` is itself wrong. The
gate approves an amendment separately from the feature, so do not fold one into
a doc. It is handed to the critique as its own value, so a doc that cites it does not
also have to prove it exists.

`responses` — nothing at all on this first pass. It exists for the passes that follow.

## What the person answered

{{.inputs.answers}}

These are the replies to the questions you raised, keyed by the `name` you gave each one.

**An answered question is settled.** Write the spec as though it had always read that
way. Do not thank them, do not record that it was asked, do not keep the question on the
doc with the answer beside it, and do not argue with it — an answer from the person the
product is for outranks your reading of the brief. Take the answer, delete the question,
and let the prose carry the decision as a plain statement of what the product does.

**An unanswered question stays open.** A key that is missing or empty means they had no
view, not that the default won. Put it back in the doc's **Open questions** table and keep
the reading you took, so the feature is still buildable.

Re-emit the deliverables in full with the answers folded in. `questions` comes back
carrying only what is still unanswered — and those belong in the doc's table now, not in
flight, because they have already been put to a person once.

## Stop arguing and ask

{{.inputs.findings}}

The critique judged that a person has to decide. This loop is not converging, and
another pass of prose will not close what is open.

**Every finding above that you cannot close from the repo becomes a `questions` entry
on this pass.** Not another paragraph defending the gap — a question, in the shape the
brief gave: `optional: true`, a `default` that is the reading you took, `type: "enum"`
with the real alternatives wherever the answer is a choice between two readings, and a
`description` saying what each answer would change.

A finding you *can* close from the repo, close — open the file and settle it. The test
is whether a `read_file` would answer it. If it would, that is not a question, it is a
read you did not do.

Rank them and keep the ones that decide something. Five a person will answer beat
fifteen they will skip.

Re-emit the deliverables in full alongside the questions, and record each finding in
`responses` as `fixed`, `rejected` or `blocked` — a finding you turned into a question
is `blocked`, with the `note` naming the question.

## What the critique said about your last draft

{{.inputs.findings}}

This is a REVISION, pass {{.inputs.iteration}}. Take each finding and either fix it,
say plainly why it is wrong, or say that you cannot see how to make progress on it —
and record which, per finding, in `responses`. A finding that comes back unchanged
twice is a finding about this state rather than about the document.

Saying you are stuck is a real answer here, not a failure. If a finding asks for
something this phase cannot produce — a measurement nobody has taken, a decision only a
person can make, a fact that is not in the repo — mark it `blocked`, and **raise it as a
`questions` entry in the same breath**. Blocked without a question is the failure: it
parks a decision nobody was asked to take. Three passes of prose defending a gap costs
more than asking once, and there is somewhere to ask.

`responses` — one entry per finding above, in the same order:

```
{ "severity": "significant",
  "claim": "<the finding, as it was put to you>",
  "target_id": "feature-name",
  "disposition": "fixed" | "rejected" | "blocked",
  "note": "what changed | why the finding is wrong | what you would need" }
```

`note` is required for `rejected` and `blocked`. This is the only memory the loop has of
its own passes: the critique reads it to tell an answered finding from a restated one.

**Re-emit the deliverables in full.** What you produced above is superseded — `features`,
`feature_docs`, `doc_paths` and the rest come back complete, not as a diff.

Two rules from the brief are the ones a revision breaks, so they are worth restating
once: the documents never mention that a revision happened, and one deliverable is
still one file. Do not open a paragraph with what the previous version said.

The docs you already opened are still open. Re-read only what a finding above puts in
question, or what another state may have edited since — re-reading the rest is the
largest single cost of a refine pass and it buys nothing.

## What the person at the gate said

{{.inputs.comments}}

A person read this and sent it back. It is a decision rather than a critique — they are
overriding a recommendation — so what they wrote is the whole of the reason, and it
outranks everything said so far in this conversation, including your own critique's
findings and your answers to them.

Do what they said. Where it conflicts with a position you argued earlier, their reading
wins and the document simply says the new thing; do not defend the old one and do not
record that it changed.

Re-emit the deliverables in full.
